summary: Defines a new object for RSVP-TE messages that carries extra attribute flags for MPLS label switched paths, since the eight-bit Flags field of the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object was nearly used up. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4420 and updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473.

plainLanguage.summary: A form with only eight tick boxes ran out of room. This memo adds a second page, so more options can be requested for a network path.

questions: what is the rsvp-te lsp_attributes object
what is the difference between lsp_attributes and lsp_required_attributes
what is the rro attributes subobject
what changed between rfc 4420 and rfc 5420
subtitle: Two new RSVP-TE objects give MPLS tunnels as many attribute flags as they need, after the old 8-bit field ran out.

tldr.problem: The Flags field in the RSVP-TE SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object has only eight bits, and almost all of them were already taken, leaving little room to signal new options for an LSP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5420 defines two objects built from TLVs, LSP_ATTRIBUTES and LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES, that carry as many attribute flags as needed. It also adds an RRO subobject that records attributes hop by hop.
tldr.outcome: Later documents can define new LSP attribute bits without touching the old field. The RFC obsoletes RFC 4420 and has since been updated by RFC 6510.

today: RFC 5420 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2009. It obsoletes RFC 4420 and updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, and it has itself been updated by RFC 6510.

sections.title: Running Out of Flag Bits
sections.content:
Traffic-engineered MPLS paths, called Label Switched Paths (LSPs), can be set up with the Path message of RSVP-TE. That message carries a SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object with a Flags field describing the options wanted for the LSP.

The field has eight bits. Three are assigned in RFC 3209 and two more in RFC 4090 for fast reroute, leaving three. Several proposals wanted those three, so the field was about to run out. RFC 5420 defines a new object, built from TLVs, that can signal further attribute bits and other attribute parameters.

The RFC rejected the simpler idea of a new C-Type for SESSION_ATTRIBUTE. Deployed implementations expect C-Type 1 or 7, so a new one would not pass transparently across legacy routers. Options already defined for SESSION_ATTRIBUTE are not migrated to the new mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The old form had eight boxes and only three were left. Instead of squeezing, the memo adds a whole new sheet that can have as many boxes as anyone needs.

sections.title: Attribute TLVs and the Flags TLV
sections.content:
Attributes travel in TLVs (type, length, value). Each TLV has a 16-bit Type and a 16-bit Length. Length counts the whole TLV, that is four plus the length of the Value field. The TLV is padded with zero to three trailing zero octets to stay four-octet aligned, and the Length does not count the padding. There are no ordering rules for TLVs.

Only one TLV type is defined: Type 1, the Attribute Flags TLV. Its Value is an array of units of 32 flags, numbered from the most significant bit as bit zero, so its Length is always a multiple of four bytes. Unassigned bits MUST be zero when sent. A bit that is missing from a short TLV, or a TLV that is absent, MUST be treated as present and set to zero.

No flag bits are defined in this document. Other RFCs that define a bit must say whether it may be set in one object, the other, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute goes in a labelled envelope that says what it is and how big it is. The only envelope so far holds a row of on/off switches, and any switch nobody mentioned counts as off.

sections.title: The LSP_ATTRIBUTES Object
sections.content:
The LSP_ATTRIBUTES object (class 197, C-Type 1) is for attributes that not every router along the path has to act on, for example ones meant only for the egress router or for border routers such as ABRs and ASBRs. Class 197 has the form 11bbbbbb, so under the RSVP rules in RFC 2205 a router that does not recognise the object forwards it unexamined and unchanged.

A router that supports the object but does not recognise a TLV type MUST pass the TLV on unaltered. A router that supports the Attribute Flags TLV but does not recognise a set bit MUST forward the TLV unchanged. If it recognises the bit but cannot support the attribute, it acts as the document defining that bit says.

The object may also appear on a Resv message to report the operational state of the whole LSP, even if the Path message had none. For example, the egress may set a bit and routers that find the status was not achieved may clear it. Because routers that do not support a bit will not clear it, each bit's use on a Resv must be fully defined by the document that defines the bit.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a note that rides along the whole route. Stops that do not understand it just pass it on, and only the stops that care read it.

sections.title: The LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES Object
sections.content:
The LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object (class 67, C-Type 1) is for attributes that MUST be inspected at every transit router. Its class number has the form 0bbbbbbb, so a router that does not recognise the object rejects the Path message with the Error Code "Unknown Object Class". It SHOULD only be used for attributes that need support at some transit routers and therefore examination at all of them.

A router that does not recognise a TLV type in this object MUST reject the Path message with a PathErr using Error Code "Unknown Attributes TLV". An unrecognised bit in the Attribute Flags TLV likewise leads to a PathErr with Error Code "Unknown Attributes Bit", with the bit number as the Error Value.

This object is not used on a Resv. Status must be reported with the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object on a Resv or with the RRO Attributes subobject.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a note marked read by everybody. If any stop cannot understand it, that stop says no and the path is not built.

sections.title: Inheritance and Per-Hop Recording
sections.content:
When a forwarding adjacency LSP is set up at a region boundary, it MAY, under local policy, inherit a subset of the Attributes TLVs. By default none of the incoming TLVs are inheritable. Documents that define bits MUST say whether they may be inherited.

To see which routers acted on a requested attribute, the RFC adds an RRO Attributes subobject to the RECORD_ROUTE object. It has Type 0x05 and a Length that is a multiple of four and at least eight, followed by attribute flags using the same bit numbers as the Attribute Flags TLV. It is pushed just before the node's IPv4, IPv6 or Unnumbered Interface ID subobject, and a node MUST NOT push it without one of those.

A router MAY set the matching bit to report compliance or clear it to report non-compliance. By default all bits SHOULD be zero, and a bit missing from a short subobject is treated as zero.
sections.plainLanguage: As the path is built, each stop can tick a box saying whether it did what was asked. The sender can read the ticks later to see who helped.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The IANA allocations made for RFC 4420 now apply to this document, and IANA updated those entries to reference RFC 5420. The two C-Nums are 197 for LSP_ATTRIBUTES and 67 for LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES, each with C-Type 1.

IANA keeps a registry of TLV types, where Type 1 is the Attribute Flags TLV allowed in both objects, and a registry of attribute bits starting at zero and continuing at least through 31. New TLV types and new bit numbers need an IETF Consensus action. The Error Codes are 29 "Unknown Attributes TLV" and 30 "Unknown Attributes Bit", and the RRO Attributes subobject has Type 5.
sections.plainLanguage: A librarian keeps the official list of which numbers mean what, so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new direct security issues and refers readers to the security considerations of RFC 2205, RFC 3209 and RFC 3473. It notes that signaling requests describing an LSP may reveal information that an administrator wants to keep secret, which can only be handled by encrypting the signaling message.

Recording attributes in the RRO may reveal the status of the LSP and the capabilities of individual routers. There is a tension between telling the head end about transit routers and hiding their existence or identity.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can read the note can learn things about the path, so secret information needs a lock on the envelope.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4420
sections.content: RFC 5420 obsoletes RFC 4420. The only technical change is in Section 3. Before, the TLV Length field counted only the Value field. Now it counts the whole TLV, which makes the format consistent with the subobject format in RFC 3209 and the TLV format in RFC 3471. The RFC Editor also made many editorial changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The size label used to measure only the inside of the box. Now it measures the whole box, like other labels already did.
